segment:
Mara remembered what Livia had said about how long Jonah had been at Fulcrum, that he was a hardware researcher, that they all liked him. None of it explained the way he looked at her. “I’m glad to meet you.”
“Welcome,” said Jonah. “This place gets interesting when Adrian comes home.” And he grinned again, but this time Mara could tell he didn’t mean it for her.
Jonah had said ‘Adrian’ the way someone might say ‘The big boss man who isn’t around right now.’ And her stomach turned over again.

It was at that moment that Mara heard people outside coming toward the common room. A familiar voice spoke, a man’s voice that sounded vaguely like Adrian. She thought she recognized another voice too, female this time.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

It was at that moment that Mara heard people outside coming toward the common room. A familiar voice spoke, a man’s voice that sounded vaguely like Adrian. She thought she recognized another voice too, female this time.

segment:
Mara felt it. She could feel him feeling it. He seemed to be wondering if she was going to say anything more.
She tried. “I—uh, didn’t know you were going to be here?”
“I usually show up early,” he answered, shifting the hand. His smile faded into uncertainty, as though he’d been caught doing something he was too polite to admit. “What do you have there?”
She looked down at her hands and saw that she still hadn’t put down the bag with her books and laptop inside.
“Nothing,” she told him, placing it on a nearby chair and coming back to the present. “Nothing but my stuff.”
His glasses didn’t hide the curiosity in his eyes. “What kind of stuff? You didn’t say anything about that.”
“Just stuff,” she said. “I have stuff in the bag. That’s what you carry your stuff in. It’s a bag for stuff.”

He turned it over a couple of times, checking out its features.
“Huh. I haven’t seen this model before. Where’d you get it?”

segment:
He released her fingers. “Would you like a drink?”
“Oh, I can—”
“Here, you can have mine.”
He went over to the bar, pulled the bottle of red from the rack and a glass from the stack, poured into it until she protested. “Thanks,” she said, taking a sip.
They stood facing each other again.
“So how long have you been here?” She gestured with her glass.
He glanced at the wall behind her and then back at her eyes. “About a week, maybe.” He gave her a smile that was definitely meant to mean something.
“I’m new, I guess,” she said, with a small laugh.
“You guess?”
“Well, yeah—it doesn’t feel like it, really. I mean…”
His eyebrows lifted; he looked at her curiously. “Interesting,” he said. Then he held out a hand to show her the way to the terrace.

segment:
She looked over his shoulder. The room had an odd, intimate feel that caught her attention: a fireplace with an unlit woodpile against one wall, the couches and low tables, all of it in subdued tones, warm light, the heavy wood walls and deep pile rugs. A library’s worth of books lined one wall; the bookshelves were interrupted only by one painting of a red-gold sunset over black waves. She turned back to face Jonah.
“Sorry. This place is just…”
He smiled.
“It’s fine. Everyone gets the same thing.” He nodded toward the window beside her and held up his wrist. “It’s six seventeen, so everyone should be trickling in soon.”
His watch was silver, elegant; she would not have thought it to be his, but he wore it as if it had always been his.

He released her hand.
“Make yourself at home,” he suggested. “I’m going to go grab a drink.” And he walked out through the doors into the hallway.
